newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi tight-lipped as summit refuses changes.
newsitem.headline: Burundi tight-lipped as summit refuses changes.

text.p: Burundi's military regime was tight-lipped on Saturday after African leaders threatened further sanctions unless it meets a one-month deadline for talks with Hutu rebels.
But the summit's refusal to make any concessions was likely to anger many in Burundi's Tutsi minority who accuse some African nations, particularly Tanzania, of siding with the Hutu majority.
"We shall study the summit's communique when we receive it and then give a measured response," a senior aide to Major Pierre Buyoya, president since a July 25 army coup, told Reuters.
Information Minister Pierre-Claver Ndayicariye said the government had no immediate comment.
Buyoya was not invited to Saturday's summit at Arusha, Tanzania, but had appealed for an easing or lifting of tough economic sanctions imposed six days after the coup.

"Overall, I think the summit decisions were positive. We were not fooling ourselves that it would be easy to get sanctions lifted," a senior officer in the mainly Tutsi army said, giving a personal response.
He said the summit's threat of unspecified measures against any armed faction that refused to join negotiations was clearly not aimed at Buyoya.
"We have agreed to such talks since we took over on July 25," he said.
The ranking member of the mainstream Hutu party Frodebu who is still inside Burundi, parliament speaker Leonce Ngendakumana, also declined to react to the summit decisions immediately.
But a senior Frodebu member, former foreign minister Venerand Bakevyumusaya, told Reuters he was disappointed that the summit had given a one-month deadline for talks.

"We are losing a lot of time by adding yet another month," he said. He and other Frodebu leaders inside the country are also opposed to the regional leaders' view that Buyoya's key Hutu interlocutor must be Leonard Nyangoma, head of the largest Hutu rebel faction.

"It is a very closed vision to be seeking negotiations with armed groups," he said. Some exiled Frodebu leaders have thrown in their lot with Nyangoma, believing that armed struggle is the only way Hutus will force minority Tutsis to share power.
Bakevyumusaya said he regretted that neither Tanzania nor Ethiopia were in the ministerial delegation the summit said it would send to Bujumbura to guage Buyoya's commitment to peace talks.

The countries chosen were Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and Cameroon. Hutu leaders say Rwanda, Burundi's northern neighbour where Tutsis also dominate the powerful army, is flouting the sanctions and silently supports Buyoya.

The senior army officer said some Tutsi extremists would be angry both with the maintenance of sanctions and with the order to talk to Nyangoma, whom they consider a Hutu bent on exterminating Tutsis.
